# Yoruba (standard orthography; dialect continuum): Lineage, root age and sibling branches

**Selection:** African language.  
**Lineage:** Niger-Congo (classification contested at highest levels) → Volta-Niger / Benue-Congo groupings vary → Yoruboid → Edekiri / Yoruba varieties.

**Root-age record:** A Cambridge overview places Niger-Congo expansion near 12,000 BP; a Language Science Press overview describes Niger-Congo as a macrofamily or phylum at least 12 millennia old while emphasizing incomplete reconstruction and uneven evidence. For the closer Yoruba lineage, Ogundiran’s interdisciplinary model places Proto-Yoruboid development in a broad 2500–300 BCE period, with daughter differentiation by about 300 CE; that window runs from roughly 4,500 to 2,300 BP.

**Evidence type:** published macrofamily expansion interpretations plus lower-level comparative classification and an archaeology / oral-history informed branch model. **Confidence:** low for an exact Niger-Congo root date or full reconstruction; low to moderate for Proto-Yoruboid calendar dates; stronger for related Yoruba, Itsekiri and Igala groupings.

**Dating limit:** The roughly 12,000 BP value is a broad family-expansion estimate, not a securely reconstructed point date for Proto-Niger-Congo. Only the early part of the Proto-Yoruboid window exceeds 2,500 years. These distinct claims should not be collapsed into a precise date for Yoruba.

| Root-age audit field | Value |
|---|---|
| Requested minimum | 2500 years BP |
| Qualifying ancestor evidence | 12000 BP |
| Reported range | not a bounded interval |
| Ancestor stage | Niger-Congo macrofamily expansion estimate; local Proto-Yoruboid chronology is reported separately |
| Assessment | qualifies only as a broad, contested macrofamily estimate; local branch date is uncertain |

**Sibling branches / comparison set:** Igala; Itsekiri / Iṣẹkiri; Yoruba varieties including Ọ̀yọ́, Èkìtì, Ìjẹ̀bú and Ìjẹ̀ṣà; Other Edekiri varieties (subgroup labels vary).

Yoruba is generally placed in Yoruboid within the Volta-Niger / Benue-Congo and broader Niger-Congo groupings. The exact higher-level classification of Niger-Congo remains debated, so the tree records commonly used labels with a warning rather than presenting every node as settled. At the lower level, comparative work treats Yoruba, Itsekiri and Igala as related Yoruboid languages; internal subgrouping and the status of varieties continue to be refined. Yoruba itself is a dialect continuum, and Standard Yoruba is a selected written norm rather than a neutral label for every regional variety.

A Cambridge overview places Niger-Congo expansion near 12,000 BP; a Language Science Press volume describes the proposed macrofamily as at least 12 millennia old. These are broad family-level interpretations. The sources also stress uneven comparative documentation, unresolved internal classification and the absence of a completed Proto-Niger-Congo lexicon and grammar. This is deep family context, not a precise Proto-Niger-Congo split date. At the closer branch level, Ogundiran’s transdisciplinary history proposes a broad Pre-Archaic period from 2500 to 300 BCE in which Proto-Yoruboid developed around the Niger–Benue confluence, followed by migration and differentiation of proto-Igala, proto-Itsekiri and proto-Yoruba by around 300 CE. Cambridge’s earlier synthesis reports very broad glottochronological estimates and stresses the last separation of Igala and Yoruba, illustrating why a precise date is not secure. The coding preserves the macrofamily age estimate and local range as different evidence records, rather than treating either as an exact date for Yoruba.

# Yoruba (standard orthography; dialect continuum): Chronology and evidence

**Selection:** African language.  
**Lineage:** Niger-Congo (classification contested at highest levels) → Volta-Niger / Benue-Congo groupings vary → Yoruboid → Edekiri / Yoruba varieties.

Yoruba has a long oral history and comparatively recent standardized writing; these evidence streams answer different questions. A Cambridge overview argues that Niger-Congo expansion likely dates to about 12,000 BP, while emphasizing the extensive work still needed to establish the macrofamily’s internal relationships and reconstructions. This is a broad expansion interpretation, not an inscription or a securely fixed ancestor date. At the closer level, the Proto-Yoruboid date in The Yoruba: A New History is a model linking linguistic, archaeological and historical evidence, not an inscription or a universally accepted clock. The Cambridge synthesis cites much wider estimates for separation of neighboring language groups. The repository retains these different time depths and confidence levels instead of selecting a single number as fact.

Latin-based Yoruba writing grew through 19th-century missionary literacy and later standardization. Sources describe 1875-era orthographic activity and a 1974 standard, with later review and continued debate over spelling and tone marking. A 2026 preprint reports a tone-marked speech corpus and concrete NFC/NFD inconsistencies, while another proposes caron/circumflex for contour tones; those marks are proposals, not part of the 1974 standard. Arabic Ajami has also been used in some Muslim communities, without one uniform standard. Standard Yoruba is consequently a social and pedagogical convention that serves readers across dialects. The timeline separates proto-language reconstruction, settlement history, manuscript/missionary practices and official spelling decisions; it does not infer an ancient script from modern diacritics.

## Dated milestones and evidence

| Date or period | Milestone | Evidence type | Confidence / limit | Sources |

| About 12,000 BP (broad literature estimate) | Niger-Congo expansion and macrofamily time depth are placed near or above this age in two scholarly overviews; internal classification and full proto-language reconstruction remain debated | historical-linguistic and interdisciplinary expansion interpretation | low to moderate; broad estimate and family-level controversy, not a precise proto-language date | [Y3](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/42051/chapter/355823946), [Y13](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781107279872.018), [Y14](https://langsci-press.org/catalog/view/190/1074/1266-2) |
| Broadly 2500–300 BCE in one model | Proto-Yoruboid develops around the Niger–Benue confluence in Ogundiran’s interdisciplinary periodization | historical model integrating archaeology, linguistics and oral history | low to moderate; not a consensus point date | [Y1](https://iupress.org/9780253051486/the-yoruba/), [Y2](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/yoruba-from-prehistory-to-the-present/geography-and-society/CC682B3D24A7A9648C018BABC1E2EDEA) |
| By c. 300 CE in the same model | Proto-Igala, Proto-Itsekiri and Proto-Yoruba differentiate | comparative linguistic and historical inference | low to moderate; model-specific | [Y1](https://iupress.org/9780253051486/the-yoruba/) |

# Yoruba (standard orthography; dialect continuum): Sound changes and historical correspondences

**Selection:** African language.  
**Lineage:** Niger-Congo (classification contested at highest levels) → Volta-Niger / Benue-Congo groupings vary → Yoruboid → Edekiri / Yoruba varieties.

Standard Yoruba is tonal, with high, mid and low tone in common analyses; mid is often unmarked (a macron can disambiguate it), while acute and grave accents mark high and low on vowels and syllabic nasals. It has seven oral vowels /i e ɛ a ɔ o u/ and nasal vowels in many descriptions, with underdots distinguishing open-mid vowels in the alphabet. The labial-velar consonants /kp/ and /gb/ are single phonemes, not onset clusters. Vowel harmony based on tongue-root contrasts is a major phonological property, but analyses of the inventory and dialect patterns differ. Tone carries lexical and grammatical information, so stripped or guessed tone is not a harmless display change.

A clear diachronic example is the change in syllable patterns under English contact. Traditional Yoruba phonology strongly favors V and CV syllables, with syllabic nasals; clusters and codas in borrowed forms are often resolved by vowel insertion or deletion. Contemporary Yoruba also shows stratified loanword patterns where clusters and codas can survive, and some hypercorrection. This is documented change, not simply “bad spelling.” Comparative Yoruboid work uses recurring correspondences among Yoruba, Itsekiri and Igala to reconstruct earlier forms; individual reconstructed segments must be tied to that comparative evidence. The code avoids inventing a complete Proto-Yoruboid sound law set where the literature is still developing.

## Documented correspondences and scoped changes

| Change | Input / environment | Outcome | Example | Scope and limitation | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Loanword cluster repair in traditional Yoruba | consonant clusters not licensed by traditional V/CV syllable patterns | often resolved by vowel epenthesis or consonant deletion | contemporary analyses compare adapted loan strata such as búrẹ́dì and brẹ́dì | Modern Yoruba has layered strata; some contemporary loans retain clusters/codas and hypercorrection occurs. | [Y6](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/canadian-journal-of-linguistics-revue-canadienne-de-linguistique/article/emerging-grammars-in-contemporary-yoruba-phonology/5FBC31A5B98304BD5F4F398569D75854) |
| Tone marking by syllable | lexical and grammatical tone in a syllable-based prosodic system | high acute, low grave, mid often unmarked in standard orthography | tone restoration performs better when syllables, rather than isolated characters, are modeled | Tone realization and marking vary by word, dialect and editorial convention. | [Y5](https://journals.agh.edu.pl/csci/article/view/2128), [Y6](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/canadian-journal-of-linguistics-revue-canadienne-de-linguistique/article/emerging-grammars-in-contemporary-yoruba-phonology/5FBC31A5B98304BD5F4F398569D75854) |
| Comparative Yoruboid correspondences | cognate forms across Yoruba, Itsekiri and Igala | reconstructed proto-segments and subgroup distinctions | Akinkugbe’s comparative phonology treats the three groups comparatively | A correspondence set must be checked in the cited reconstruction; this module does not invent a general proto-to-modern substitution. | [Y4](https://journalofwestafricanlanguages.org/downloads/summary/31-volume1101/131-an-internal-classification-of-the-yoruboid-group-yoruba-isekiri-igala) |

# Yoruba (standard orthography; dialect continuum): Syllable structure, prosody and sentence patterns

**Selection:** African language.  
**Lineage:** Niger-Congo (classification contested at highest levels) → Volta-Niger / Benue-Congo groupings vary → Yoruboid → Edekiri / Yoruba varieties.

Traditional Yoruba syllables are commonly analyzed as V, CV, and syllabic nasal; clusters and codas are disallowed in the conservative core phonology. The contemporary lexicon is more layered: English loans and contact can introduce clusters and coda patterns, which may be repaired, retained or hypercorrected depending on lexical history and speaker practice. Tone is associated with syllables and can distinguish words or grammatical forms. Syllable-sensitive tone restoration research found that syllabic units improved automatic tone-mark restoration compared with character-only approaches, which is practical evidence that orthography and phonology must be modeled above the code-point level.

Yoruba is commonly described as SVO, with preverbal markers and serial verb constructions. Clause meaning also depends on tone, particles and information structure. The standard writing norm uses acute for high tone, grave for low, and often leaves mid unmarked; absence of a mark in printed text can reflect editorial omission rather than the word having no tone. Dialect differences and contact mean one template cannot be applied mechanically to all speech. The profile therefore distinguishes traditional syllable structure from emerging contemporary patterns, and standard orthography from an unmarked keyboard transcript.

## Compact structural record

| Feature | Summary |
|---|---|
| Syllable profile | Traditional V/CV plus syllabic nasal; tone-bearing syllables; contemporary contact has expanded some loanword strata with clusters and codas. |
| Sentence pattern | Broadly SVO with preverbal grammatical markers, serial verbs, tone and information-structure effects. |

# Yoruba (standard orthography; dialect continuum): Script, glyph change and Unicode

**Selection:** African language.  
**Lineage:** Niger-Congo (classification contested at highest levels) → Volta-Niger / Benue-Congo groupings vary → Yoruboid → Edekiri / Yoruba varieties.

Yoruba is written primarily in an adapted Latin alphabet. Standard letters Ẹ/ẹ, Ọ/ọ and Ṣ/ṣ distinguish sounds; tone marks above vowels and syllabic nasals indicate high (acute) and low (grave), while mid tone is often unmarked or shown with a macron for disambiguation. The underdot is a below-base diacritic that identifies a different letter value; it is not a subscript letter. A tone mark and an underdot can occur on the same vowel, so rendering needs a font with correct stacking. Some communities have used Arabic Ajami, but there is no single uniform Ajami standard for all Yoruba text.

Unicode examples include Ẹ U+1EB8, ẹ U+1EB9, Ọ U+1ECC, ọ U+1ECD, Ṣ U+1E62 and ṣ U+1E63. An acute can be U+0301 and grave U+0300; underdots can be represented in sequences with U+0323, although precomposed underdotted letters are also available. For example, e + dot below + acute can normalize to ẹ + acute. NFC/NFD may therefore produce different code-point sequences that render as the same grapheme. A 2026 preprint describes normalization failures in more than 60% of lines in a 24,905-sentence tone-marked corpus. A separate 2026 preprint proposes caron/circumflex as optional contour-tone marks; these are not standard orthography. Preserve underdots and tone marks in canonical text; do not strip accents for search storage. The writing system has no native subscript letters. Unicode encodes marks and abstract characters, not the hand strokes of manuscript or print glyphs.

## Script and encoding inventory

| Sequence | Code points | Role / reading note |
|---|---|---|
| `Ẹ` | `U+1EB8` | capital E with dot below |
| `ẹ` | `U+1EB9` | small e with dot below |
| `Ṣ` | `U+1E62` | capital S with dot below |
| `ṣ` | `U+1E63` | small s with dot below |
| `ẹ́` | `U+1EB9 + U+0301` | precomposed underdotted e plus combining acute |
| `ẹ́` | `U+0065 + U+0323 + U+0301` | decomposed base, dot below, acute; normalize carefully |
| `ń` | `U+0144` | small n with acute; high tone on a syllabic nasal |
| `ǹ` | `U+01F9` | small n with grave; low tone on a syllabic nasal |
| `n̄` | `U+006E + U+0304` | n plus combining macron; mid tone may be marked to disambiguate |
| `ǎ` | `U+0061 + U+030C` | base a plus combining caron, shown only as a proposed contour-tone notation |

### Major writing-system stages

| Stage |
|---|
| Pre-standard oral and manuscript traditions |
| 19th-century missionary Latin literacy |
| Orthography standardization in 1875-era and later work |
| 1974 standard and ongoing digital/educational conventions |
| 2026 digital corpus and proposed contour-tone notation |

**Normalization:** Support both precomposed and combining sequences; NFC is convenient, but compare normalized grapheme sequences. Never drop underdots or tone marks from canonical Yoruba text.

**Subscript status:** Underdots are combining diacritics, not subscript letters. No native subscript letters in standard Yoruba orthography.

**Glyph / stroke note:** Underdots and stacked tone marks change the letter/grapheme distinction. Handwritten dots, printed marks and font placement vary; Unicode records code points and combining behavior, not physical stroke order. A 2026 proposal uses caron/circumflex for contour tones, but that is not the 1974 standard.

## Sources

# Spanish: Latin descent, Romance siblings and spelling
Latin inscriptions attest the ancestor by the 7th–6th c. BCE. Spanish later developed from regional spoken Latin over centuries. Romance siblings include Portuguese/Galician, Astur-Leonese, Aragonese, Catalan (classification debated), French, Italian, Sardinian and Romanian. Latin’s case endings eroded; prepositions, clitics and word order grew in importance.

Latin script reached Rome through Etruscan adaptation of Greek. Ancient capitals, book hands, cursive and medieval minuscule differ in glyph and stroke practice. Ñ is a letter; ch/ll are digraphs. Unicode: ñ U+00F1, Ñ U+00D1; acute vowels U+00E1, E9, ED, F3, FA; ü U+00FC; ¿ U+00BF and ¡ U+00A1. Accents may be precomposed or decomposed combining sequences. No native subscripts.

Spanish has five vowels; common syllable form (C)(C)V(C), stress rules depend on word ending and accents. SVO is common but order is flexible and subjects may be omitted. Castilian initial Latin f often developed via h to zero (farina > harina, filium > hijo); stressed Latin short e/o often became ie/ue (terra > tierra, porta > puerta). These inherited sound changes have exceptions and regional scope.

Sources: [Cambridge Italic](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/indoeuropean-language-family/italic/473A395FABB6E9FB91AE75076F390D29); [Latin script](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/latin-palaeography/latin-script-in-antiquity/7AAE013BCD262AB689DE4B2FAAD02B0D); [Oxford From Latin to Romance](https://academic.oup.com/book/26021); [Spanish syllable](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/cambridge-handbook-of-spanish-linguistics/syllable/CB48DEE6ECF4EAD91E816486BA8E8573).\n

Yoruba is Volta-Niger/Yoruboid; siblings include Itsekiri and Igala, with internal subgrouping debated.
